tagline: Prairie gives way to forest on the road to the Mississippi headwaters.
intro: Prairie grasslands give way to hardwoods and conifers as the Lake Country Scenic Byway heads east across Minnesota. Its 88 miles link Detroit Lakes, Park Rapids and Walker, with a northern spur to Itasca State Park. The Lake Country Scenic Byway Association highlights that changing vegetation alongside lakes, rivers, public forests and recreational trails. Pine and hardwood forest alternate with lakes, meadows and farmland. A wayside west of Osage offers a stop among pines, while the road also follows part of Minnesota’s Pine to Prairie Birding Trail.

Highway 34 was established in 1920, and by 1930 its entire length was graveled. In 1941, a new alignment through Snellman made the road to Osage more direct, replacing a route along Shell Lake and through Ponsford. The realigned section was paved in 1946. Lake Country received state byway designation in 1999. Through Park Rapids, the highway expanded to five lanes in 2008.

From Detroit Lakes, Highway 34 crosses the Smoky Hills State Forest on the way to Park Rapids. There, Highway 71 branches north to Itasca State Park and the Mississippi headwaters. Returning to the eastbound route brings Nevis and Akeley, then the Chippewa National Forest before Walker. Walker sits on Leech Lake’s southwest corner.
notice: In June, showy lady’s slippers bloom along Highway 34’s south side from the Height of Land Lake area to east of Snellman.

moments.title: Itasca State Park
moments.text: At Lake Itasca’s north end, a 44-foot outlet dam defines the Mississippi headwaters. In 1832, Anishinaabe guide Ozaawindib led Henry Schoolcraft to this source of the river. Later, surveyor Jacob V. Brower saw logging transforming the region and campaigned to protect the remaining pine forest. His work led to the park’s creation in 1891, approved by the state legislature by a single vote. Some of Itasca’s red pines are more than 200 years old. The park’s forest also includes aspen and birch on logged pine land, with aspen now its most abundant tree species.

moments.title: Akeley
moments.text: Akeley’s Paul Bunyan kneels beside a giant cradle, a 25-foot figure in a town built on lumber. T. B. Walker and Healy C. Akeley formed the Red River Lumber Company in 1893 and largely developed the town. A train depot arrived in 1899, followed by Walker’s sawmill in 1902; together they made Akeley a boomtown. The population grew from 2,000 to more than 3,500 between 1907 and 1908. The Paul Bunyan Historical Museum holds pictures and artifacts from the community’s early years. The town has celebrated Paul Bunyan Days since 1955.

moments.title: Walker
moments.text: Walker’s name was an invitation to a lumberman. Patrick McGarry founded the town in 1896 after the railroad arrived, naming it for Thomas B. Walker in hopes of attracting a sawmill. That operation went to Akeley, while four other logging companies helped Walker develop. Tourism later grew as visitors came for fishing, hunting and water sports. On Leech Lake’s southwest corner, the town now has the Paul Bunyan State Trail passing along the lake. The Cass County Historical Society operates a museum and research center in town, interpreting the county’s history.
